data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The distinguishing evidence within a single evaluation is a dissociation between checklist adherence and outcome on the single expert's domain of strength: if the panel achieves high accuracy with low checklist adherence on those items, it indicates genuine competence; if it achieves high accuracy only with high checklist adherence, it indicates mere compliance.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the panel is trained to always follow the checklist, adherence will be uniformly high, making the dissociation unobservable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert's 'domain of strength' is not identifiable within the evaluation, this subset cannot be defined.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the checklist is perfectly correlated with the expert's strength, the dissociation is structurally impossible.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The expert's intuition is assumed to be strong on some subset of items. If the panel, on those same items, can succeed without strictly following the checklist, it means the panel's non-experts have acquired (via training) some of the expert's competence, not just the checklist. If they succeed only when they follow the checklist, their success is mechanistically tied to the checklist, i.e., mere compliance. So the within-evaluation evidence is the interaction term between checklist adherence, panel success, and item type (expert-strength vs not).","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
